case_title: Arnesh Kumar v. State of Bihar
holding: Arrest must not be automatic merely because an offence is cognizable. For offences punishable with under seven years, the police must first satisfy the arrest conditions and, where arrest is unnecessary, issue a notice of appearance instead. Officers who arrest without recording reasons expose themselves to departmental action.

case_title: D.K. Basu v. State of West Bengal
holding: The Court laid down binding safeguards for every arrest and detention, including a signed and witnessed memo of arrest, informing a relative or friend, and periodic medical examination of the arrestee. Failure to follow these requirements invites contempt and departmental consequences. The directions apply to all agencies exercising powers of arrest.

case_title: Joginder Kumar v. State of Uttar Pradesh
holding: The power to arrest and the justification for exercising it are distinct questions. An officer must be able to show a reasonable basis and the necessity for the arrest, and the arrested person is entitled to have a nominated person informed of the detention.

case_title: Satender Kumar Antil v. Central Bureau of Investigation
holding: The Court grouped offences into categories and issued consolidated directions on when bail should ordinarily follow, stressing that arrest should not be used as a routine investigative step. It reiterated that non-compliance with the arrest-notice provisions weighs in favour of releasing the accused.

case_title: Siddharth v. State of Uttar Pradesh
holding: An investigating officer is not obliged to arrest an accused merely in order to file the charge sheet, where the accused has cooperated throughout the investigation. Courts should not insist on custody as a precondition for accepting a final report.

case_title: Prem Shankar Shukla v. Delhi Administration
holding: Routine handcuffing of an undertrial is unconstitutional; restraints may be used only where there is clear and recorded justification such as a demonstrable risk of escape or violence. The escorting officer must record reasons and, where practicable, obtain judicial sanction.

case_title: Nandini Satpathy v. P.L. Dani
holding: The protection against self-incrimination extends to the investigation stage and not merely to trial, so an accused may decline to answer questions that could expose them to a criminal charge. The Court also recognised the value of allowing legal assistance during police questioning.

case_title: Selvi v. State of Karnataka
holding: Narcoanalysis, polygraph and brain-mapping tests cannot be administered to a suspect without free and informed consent, as compelled testimonial responses offend the protection against self-incrimination. Material discovered subsequently and independently may still be admissible.

case_title: Rakesh Kumar Paul v. State of Assam
holding: Where the investigation is not completed within the statutory period, the accused acquires an indefeasible right to default bail on applying and being prepared to furnish bail. The right does not depend on the accused using any particular form of words in the application.

case_title: Bikramjit Singh v. State of Punjab
holding: The right to default bail on expiry of the permitted investigation period is a fundamental right traceable to personal liberty and cannot be defeated by filing the charge sheet after the application is made. It is available before the court competent to take cognizance at that stage.

case_title: Anvar P.V. v. P.K. Basheer
holding: Electronic records produced as secondary evidence are inadmissible unless accompanied by the statutory certificate identifying the device and the manner of production. The Court held that the special provision for electronic evidence overrides the general secondary-evidence provisions, and departed from the contrary view taken in the Parliament attack case.

case_title: Arjun Panditrao Khotkar v. Kailash Kushanrao Gorantyal
holding: A larger bench confirmed that the certificate for electronic records is a mandatory precondition to admissibility of secondary electronic evidence, and clarified when it may be dispensed with because the original device itself is produced. It expressly disapproved the relaxation suggested in an earlier two-judge ruling and gave directions on obtaining the certificate from a reluctant custodian.

case_title: Shafhi Mohammad v. State of Himachal Pradesh
holding: This two-judge ruling suggested that the electronic-evidence certificate could be relaxed for a party not in possession of the device. It has since been expressly overruled by a larger bench and must not be relied on as the current position of law; it is retained here so that officers recognise and avoid citing it.

case_title: State (NCT of Delhi) v. Navjot Sandhu
holding: The Court admitted call records as secondary evidence without the statutory electronic-records certificate. That specific holding on electronic evidence was later overruled, though the judgment remains significant on other aspects of conspiracy and confession evidence.

case_title: Ritesh Sinha v. State of Uttar Pradesh
holding: A judicial magistrate may direct an accused to give a voice sample for comparison during investigation, and this does not violate the protection against self-incrimination because a voice exemplar is identificatory rather than testimonial. The Court invoked its plenary powers pending legislative provision.

case_title: Pulukuri Kottaya v. Emperor
holding: Only so much of a statement made in police custody as distinctly relates to the fact thereby discovered is admissible; the confessional remainder must be excluded. This decision remains the foundational authority on the scope of discovery-based statements and is routinely applied to recovery panchnamas.

case_title: Mohd. Inayatullah v. State of Maharashtra
holding: The Court set out the conditions for admitting a discovery statement: a fact must be actually discovered in consequence of information from an accused in custody, and only the portion distinctly relating to that discovery is usable. The provision is an exception to the general bar on custodial statements and must be construed strictly.

case_title: State of Uttar Pradesh v. Deoman Upadhyaya
holding: The Court upheld the constitutional validity of admitting discovery statements made to police, holding the classification between persons in custody and others to be reasonable. It affirmed that the discovery provision is a carefully limited exception rather than a general licence to prove custodial statements.

case_title: State of Rajasthan v. Teja Ram
holding: Recovery evidence should not be discarded merely because of lapses by the investigating officer or because the seizure witnesses turned hostile, where the recovery itself is otherwise established. Courts should evaluate whether the defect actually causes prejudice rather than treating every irregularity as fatal.

case_title: Trimbak v. State of Madhya Pradesh
holding: Where stolen property is recovered from an open place accessible to others, exclusive possession by the accused is not established and the presumption arising from recent possession cannot safely be drawn. The place and circumstances of recovery must therefore be recorded with precision in the seizure panchnama.

case_title: Gulab Chand v. State of Madhya Pradesh
holding: Recent and unexplained possession of stolen articles allows a court to presume either that the possessor committed the theft or that they received the goods knowing them stolen, depending on the surrounding circumstances. The strength of the presumption weakens as the interval between the offence and the recovery grows.

case_title: Pyare Lal Bhargava v. State of Rajasthan
holding: Theft is complete on dishonestly moving property out of another's possession without consent, even if the taker intends to return it later. Temporary deprivation of the owner's use is sufficient to constitute the offence.

case_title: K.N. Mehra v. State of Rajasthan
holding: Dishonest intention at the moment of taking is the essence of theft, and a temporary appropriation causing wrongful loss to the owner suffices. The offence does not require an intention to keep the property permanently.

case_title: Sharad Birdhichand Sarda v. State of Maharashtra
holding: In a case resting on circumstantial evidence the proved circumstances must be fully established, consistent only with guilt, and incapable of explanation on any other reasonable hypothesis. These five conditions form the standard test applied whenever there is no direct eyewitness to the offence.

case_title: Hanumant v. State of Madhya Pradesh
holding: Circumstantial evidence must form a chain so complete that it excludes every reasonable hypothesis other than the guilt of the accused. Suspicion, however strong, cannot substitute for proof.

case_title: Malkhansingh v. State of Madhya Pradesh
holding: A test identification parade is a step in the investigation meant to corroborate identification in court; it is not substantive evidence by itself. Its absence does not automatically render the identification in court unreliable, though a parade should ordinarily be held promptly where the accused is unknown to the witness.

case_title: Dana Yadav alias Dahu v. State of Bihar
holding: Identification for the first time in court, without a prior parade, carries reduced weight unless supported by convincing reasons or corroboration. Delay in holding a parade after arrest materially reduces its evidentiary value.

case_title: Vadivelu Thevar v. State of Madras
holding: Conviction may rest on the testimony of a single witness if that testimony is wholly reliable; the law weighs the quality of evidence rather than counting witnesses. Where testimony is neither wholly reliable nor wholly unreliable, the court should look for corroboration.

case_title: Sat Paul v. Delhi Administration
holding: The evidence of a witness who has been declared hostile is not automatically wiped out; the court may rely on such parts of it as are found trustworthy and corroborated. The whole testimony must be examined with care rather than discarded wholesale.

case_title: Appabhai v. State of Gujarat
holding: Courts should recognise the practical reluctance of independent bystanders to associate themselves with police proceedings, and should not reject prosecution evidence merely because independent panch witnesses were not produced. The evidence must instead be assessed on its intrinsic worth.

case_title: Masalti v. State of Uttar Pradesh
holding: Evidence of an interested or partisan witness is not to be rejected on that ground alone, but must be scrutinised with care before being accepted. Mechanical tests such as requiring a fixed number of corroborating witnesses are inappropriate.

case_title: State of Punjab v. Baldev Singh
holding: A person about to be searched under the narcotics law must be informed of the right to be searched before a gazetted officer or magistrate, and failure to do so vitiates the recovery for the purpose of conviction. The Court stressed that statutory search safeguards are mandatory rather than directory.

case_title: State of Punjab v. Balbir Singh
holding: The Court explained which search and seizure requirements under the narcotics law are mandatory and which are procedural, and the consequences of non-compliance for the resulting recovery. Compliance must be demonstrable from the contemporaneous record rather than asserted later.

case_title: Directorate of Revenue v. Mohammed Nisar Holia
holding: Statutory safeguards attached to search of a person or premises reflect the constitutional protection of privacy and must be strictly observed by the searching officer. Recovery obtained in disregard of those safeguards is liable to be viewed with suspicion.

case_title: Lalita Kumari v. Government of Uttar Pradesh
holding: Registration of a first information report is mandatory when the information discloses a cognizable offence, and no preliminary inquiry is permissible in such a case. A limited preliminary inquiry is allowed only in specified categories where it is unclear whether a cognizable offence is made out.

case_title: State of Haryana v. Bhajan Lal
holding: The Court set out the categories of cases in which a criminal proceeding or FIR may be quashed by the High Court, such as where the allegations even if accepted disclose no offence. It cautioned that this power is to be exercised sparingly and not to weigh evidence at the threshold.

case_title: Thulia Kali v. State of Tamil Nadu
holding: Unexplained delay in lodging the first information report is a significant circumstance because it allows time for deliberation and embellishment. The prosecution must offer a satisfactory explanation for the delay.

case_title: H.N. Rishbud v. State of Delhi
holding: An irregularity or illegality in the conduct of an investigation does not by itself vitiate the resulting trial unless the accused shows prejudice. The proper course is to direct reinvestigation where the defect is noticed before trial concludes.

case_title: Sanjay Chandra v. Central Bureau of Investigation
holding: Bail is the rule and committal to custody the exception, and pre-trial detention must not be used as a punishment where the accused is unlikely to abscond or tamper with evidence. The seriousness of the accusation alone does not justify indefinite custody.

case_title: Gurbaksh Singh Sibbia v. State of Punjab
holding: The power to grant anticipatory bail is not to be confined by rigid judge-made conditions and should be exercised on the facts of each case. The Court declined to read in blanket limitations such as a fixed duration or a requirement of exceptional circumstances.

case_title: Sunil Batra v. Delhi Administration
holding: Prisoners retain their fundamental rights subject only to the necessary incidents of lawful confinement, and measures such as solitary confinement or bar fetters require justification and judicial oversight. Custodial practice must remain within constitutional limits.
